summary:
AresPath is a real-time, multi-layered tactical navigation and hazard interface designed specifically for astronauts during Martian surface Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). While orbital satellite maps help mission control plan routes, they lack the local ground-level detail and instant feedback needed by astronauts wearing bulky spacesuits.
​By fusing NASA orbital elevation data with live suit sensors and zero-delay edge AI, AresPath projects safe walking paths, highlights dangerous terrain like steep slopes or loose dunes, flags high-priority scientific rock formations, and delivers instant voice and visual alerts for radiation spikes or dust storms. This eliminates Earth-to-Mars communication lag, maximizing astronaut survival and scientific discovery at Jezero Crater and future planetary missions.
details:
How It Works:

AresPath is an interactive, multi-layered Martian EVA navigation and survival guide designed for real-time astronaut field use. It combines high-resolution NASA orbital elevation and terrain datasets (such as Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE imagery and MOLA topography) with live spacesuit telemetry and local edge AI processing. Instead of relying solely on static overhead maps from Mission Control, astronauts receive a dynamic heads-up terrain overlay showing safe walking corridors, slope gradients, loose regolith hazards, and high-priority geological sampling sites at Jezero Crater.

​Benefits & Intended Impact:

Because Earth-to-Mars radio communication delays range from 4 to 24 minutes each way, astronauts cannot wait for Earth-based guidance during sudden surface emergencies. AresPath eliminates communication lag by computing safe rerouting paths and triggering instant visual and audio alerts for radiation spikes, dust storm fronts, and oxygen-to-base return thresholds—dramatically improving crew survival and scientific productivity.

​Tools, Creativity & Key Factors Considered:

We built the interactive map concept and data pipeline using Python for terrain slope/hazard modeling, standard web/UI prototyping tools for the astronaut heads-up display, and open NASA planetary datasets. Key human factors considered include high-contrast colorblind-safe hazard markers for dusty lighting conditions, simplified hands-free voice alerts suited for pressurized spacesuits, and strict battery/oxygen margin calculations.
